title: A plant RNA-binding protein senses 2',3'-cNMP produced by insect effectors.
abstract: RNA-derived 2',3'-cyclophosphate-terminated nucleotides act as immune signalling molecules in prokaryotes and eukaryotes1-3, but how plants perceive them remains unknown. Sucking insects inject digestive enzymes including RNases into the host plant to acquire nutrients. Here we demonstrate that NIB1, a glycine-rich RNA-binding protein in rice, senses 2',3'-cyclic nucleotide monophosphates (2',3'-cNMPs; 2',3'-cAMP and 2',3'-cGMP) and adenylyl-(3'→5')-guanosine 2',3'-cyclic phosphate (ApG>p) produced by a salivary T2 ribonuclease of green stink bug during feeding. Binding of the RNase products promotes formation of nuclear condensates containing NIB1, which recruit the core immune regulator Enhanced Disease Susceptibility 1 (EDS1) and activate defence, potentially contributing to the immune signalling of Toll/interleukin-1 receptor (TIR) proteins that also produce the nuclease products. Exogenous application of 2',3'-cAMP, 2',3'-cGMP or ApG>p elicits NIB1 and EDS1-mediated immune responses. Our findings unveil a conserved pathway in plants, in which glycine-rich RNA-binding proteins perceive the nuclease-generated second messengers to launch defence and point to a potential link between plant TIR nuclease activity and EDS1 signalling.

title: SecAntiGami: A Secondary-Antibody-Inspired RNA Origami for Qualitative Aptamer Validation.
abstract: RNA aptamers are short, single-stranded RNA molecules that fold into specific three-dimensional structures and selectively bind molecular targets. Despite applications in therapeutics, diagnostics, and biosensing, tools for aptamer validation remain scarce compared to well-established pipelines for other biomolecular binders such as antibodies. Here, we introduce SecAntiGami─a secondary-antibody-inspired RNA origami─as a modular tool for signal enhancement and aptamer characterization. SecAntiGami binds aptamers of interest through programmable kissing-loop interactions and carries a fluorescent aptamer for visualization. It amplifies aptamer-dependent size increases in dynamic light scattering assays and enables fluorescence-based aptamer localization. We rationally design three different variants of a biotin-binding aptamer and use SecAntiGami to demonstrate that all of them retain their functionality, enabling efficient integration of aptamers into RNA origami structures. SecAntiGami serves as a versatile tool for qualitative aptamer validation for synthetic biology, structural RNA nanotechnology, RNA therapeutics, and diagnostics.

title: Transcriptional boosting and buffering during neurodevelopment by shifts in mRNA instability.
abstract: The contribution of mRNA half-life is commonly overlooked when examining changes in mRNA abundance during development. mRNA levels are regulated by transcription rate or mRNA half-life, but combinations of both could boost or buffer the final steady-state. We measured transcription rate and mRNA half-life changes during human induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC)-derived neuronal development using RATE-seq. The most prevalent mode of gene regulation during transitions to neuronal progenitors and neurons was transcriptional buffering. Less prevalent modes consisted of transcriptional boosting events, transcription rate only shifts, or mRNA half-life only shifts. Buffered and novel boosted gene sets were enriched in RNA-binding protein (RBP) motifs and microRNA sites. Global mRNA half-life decreased two-fold in neurons. microRNA copy number per cell increased during neurodevelopment coincident with destabilization of a subset of short isoforms that contributed to increased average 3'UTR length. Our findings identify mRNA instability mechanisms that regulate transcript levels and 3'UTR isoform abundance, and provide a precedent for transcriptional boosting or buffering during development of other human tissues.

title: Simple models outperform single-cell foundation models on downstream benchmarks
abstract: Single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) data exhibit strong and reproducible statistical structure. This has motivated the development of large-scale foundation models, such as TranscriptFormer, that use transformer-based architectures to learn a generative model for gene expression by embedding genes into a latent vector space. These embeddings have been used to obtain state-of-the-art (SOTA) performance on downstream tasks such as cell-type classification, disease-state prediction, and cross-species learning. Here, we ask whether similar performance can be achieved without utilizing computationally intensive deep learning-based representations. Using simple, interpretable pipelines that rely on careful normalization and linear methods, we obtain SOTA or near SOTA performance across multiple benchmarks commonly used to evaluate single-cell foundation models, including outperforming foundation models on out-of-distribution tasks involving novel cell types and organisms absent from the training data. Our findings highlight the need for rigorous benchmarking and suggest that the biology of cell identity can be captured by simple linear representations of single cell gene expression data.

title: HIV-1 excludes non-guanosine nucleotides in major transcription start sites to ensure distinct unspliced RNA fates.
abstract: HIV-1 expresses two unspliced RNA transcripts with distinct 5' untranslated region (UTR) structures-one optimized for packaging to serve as the viral genome and the other optimized to serve as an mRNA template for translation. This strategy requires precisely regulated production of two structurally distinct RNA isoforms, yet the mechanisms controlling this regulation remain poorly understood. In this work, we targeted the three guanosines in the HIV-1 genome that serve as start sites for the major transcripts and examined the impact of specific nucleotide substitutions on RNA expression, the resulting RNA structures, and viral replication. Our studies demonstrate that substituting the guanosines with pyrimidines severely perturbs transcription initiation from these sites. Adenosine substitutions are well tolerated as initiation sites for RNA polymerase II but eliminate the distinct post-transcriptional fates of the resulting transcripts through a structure-based mechanism. This work provides insights into the evolutionary pressures on HIV-1 to maintain three guanosines as major transcription start sites and the finely tuned regulation of HIV-1 RNA that ensures production of two structurally and functionally distinct unspliced RNAs. To optimize replication fitness, HIV-1 expresses two major unspliced transcripts that are 99.9% identical, yet perform distinct functions. These transcripts are initiated at guanosines two nucleotides apart within the 5'-long terminal repeat (LTR). Through genetic and structural studies, we show that these guanosines serve two regulatory roles. At the DNA level, they control transcription initiation of the two RNA isoforms. At the RNA level, they control the interplay of two RNA hairpins at the start of the 5'-untranslated region, leading to divergent global RNA structures. This elegant mechanism enables functionally distinct transcripts to arise from nearly identical sequences and highlights how evolutionary pressures act at both the DNA and RNA levels to preserve guanosine identity at the major transcription start sites.

title: RBM33 is a unique m6A RNA-binding protein that regulates ALKBH5 demethylase activity and substrate selectivity.
Transection of the cervical sympathetic trunk ameliorates pulmonary arterial hypertension by reprogramming transcription factor networks and alternative splicing in rat model.
abstract: Transection of the cervical sympathetic trunk (TCST) ameliorates pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH), but the molecular mechanisms remain unclear. This study aimed to elucidate these mechanisms in monocrotaline (MCT)-induced PAH rats through transcriptomic profiling. PAH rats were divided into control, PAH, PAH + sham, and PAH + TCST groups. Therapeutic effects were evaluated by hemodynamics and histology. RNA-seq was performed on lung tissues to identify differentially expressed genes (DEGs), followed by transcription factor (TF) network analysis and alternative splicing analysis, with validation by qPCR and ELISA. TCST significantly reduced mPAP, RVSP, and RVHI, and attenuated vascular remodeling. RNA-seq identified 500 DEGs (61 upregulated, 439 downregulated). TF network analysis revealed that target genes of differentially expressed TFs were enriched in inflammation, proliferation, and calcium signaling. Multiple PAH-associated genes (Bmp2, Ptgs2, Cxcl13, Wnt7b, Tacr1, Adra1d) were downregulated following TCST. Alternative splicing analysis showed that TCST modulated RNA-binding protein (RBP) expression and altered splicing patterns of PAH-relevant genes (Aldh2, Il1rn, Foxm1). qPCR and ELISA confirmed suppression of the Foxa3/Adra1d-Tacr1 axis and reduced IP3 production. TCST exerts therapeutic effects through selective reprogramming of TF networks and regulation of RBP-mediated alternative splicing, coordinately suppressing PAH-associated pathways at transcriptional and post-transcriptional levels. These findings provide mechanistic insights and a theoretical basis for developing neuromodulatory strategies for PAH.

title: FlAsH-ID enables live-cell photoproximity labeling with a short peptide tag.
abstract: Proximity labeling has emerged as a valuable tool for the interrogation of protein-protein and protein-RNA interactions. Almost all proximity labeling methods are deployed using large fusion proteins, which, while powerful in many contexts, can disrupt native biology or obscure important epitopes on the protein under study. Here we develop a photoproximity labeling method that is localized to a short 6-aa peptide sequence. Termed FlAsH-ID, this method uses the combination of the Tsien tetracysteine tag with the FlAsH dye for localized singlet oxygen generation. We demonstrate that this green-light-based method is nontoxic and can be used to label proteins within several cellular compartments. Lastly, we establish that FlAsH-ID can be deployed in primary CD8+ T cells to assess the interactome of the transcription factor RUNX3. Our results suggest this technique will expand the field of proximity labeling to small, functionally sensitive proteins in primary cells without perturbing their function.

title: The Numb paradox: one protein, multiple isoforms, opposing functions in neurodevelopment, endocytic trafficking, and cancer.
abstract: Numb is a multifunctional adaptor protein that serves as a central regulator of cell fate, linking polarity, signaling, and endocytic trafficking from early development to disease. Initially discovered in Drosophila melanogaster as an intrinsic determinant of asymmetric cell division, Numb's antagonism of Notch signaling has proven to be evolutionarily conserved in mammals, orchestrating the balance between progenitor maintenance and differentiation during neurogenesis. In the mammalian brain, Numb and its paralog, Numb-like (Numbl), integrate polarity cues, receptor trafficking, and transcriptional networks to guide cortical development and maintain neural stem cell homeostasis. Alternative splicing generates multiple Numb isoforms (i.e., p72, p71, p66, and p65) that exhibit distinct structural and functional properties, allowing context-dependent modulation of Notch, p53, and integrin pathways. Isoform-specific expression patterns underlie divergent roles in neurodevelopment, neurite morphogenesis, and tumorigenesis, whereby Numb can act either as a tumor suppressor or as an oncogenic driver. Dysregulated splicing, posttranslational modification, and interaction with RNA-binding proteins such as RBM4, PTBP1, or SRSF9 reprogram Numb's activity across developmental and cancer contexts. Emerging evidence also connects Numb isoform regulation to neurodegenerative processes, including tauopathies and viral neuropathogenesis, as observed in Zika virus infection. Collectively, these findings position Numb as a molecular switch at the crossroads of neurodevelopment, cancer, and degeneration with its isoform diversity providing both mechanistic insight and therapeutic potential for restoring differentiation, restraining oncogenesis, and protecting neuronal integrity.

title: Comprehensive identification of lactate metabolism-related genes in recurrent spontaneous abortion: An observational study integrating bioinformatics and experimental validation.
abstract: Recurrent spontaneous abortion (RSA) is a complex multifactorial disease. Lactate metabolism (LM) has been implicated in RSA pathogenesis, but the underlying molecular mechanisms remain unclear. This observational study aimed to identify key LM-related genes (LM-RGs) in RSA and explore their potential regulatory mechanisms and therapeutic targets. The study combined bioinformatics analysis with experimental validation. The training dataset GSE26787 and validation dataset GSE165004 were obtained from the Gene Expression Omnibus database. Differentially expressed genes were identified using the limma package. Candidate LM-RGs were obtained by intersecting differentially expressed genes with 262 LM-RGs from the Gene Set Enrichment Analysis database. Hub genes were identified through protein-protein interaction network analysis using the CytoHubba plugin (National Cheng Kung University). Key genes were further screened using Boruta and random forest machine learning algorithms, followed by expression validation in both Gene Expression Omnibus datasets. Reverse transcription-quantitative polymerase chain reaction was performed on 10 RSA and 10 control endometrial samples to validate key gene expression. Gene set enrichment analysis and gene set variation analysis were conducted to explore functional pathways. Regulatory networks involving microRNAs, long noncoding RNAs, and transcription factors were constructed, and potential therapeutic drugs were predicted using the Drug Signatures Database. CALR (upregulated) and PIEZO1 (downregulated) were identified as key genes in RSA and were functionally linked to pathways such as cytokine signaling. Furthermore, we delineated a regulatory network governing these genes, implicating the long noncoding RNA X-inactive specific transcript and shared transcription factors, including MYC proto-oncogene, bHLH transcription factor and vitamin D receptor. We propose several candidate drugs, including estradiol, predicted to target both CALR and PIEZO1. This study identifies CALR and PIEZO1 as key LM-RGs in RSA, with significant dysregulation confirmed in clinical samples. These genes are involved in cytokine signaling pathways and are regulated by complex molecular networks. The identification of common targeting drugs provides a foundation for developing novel therapeutic strategies for RSA. Further studies are warranted to validate these findings and explore their clinical applications.

title: Truncated APC regulates alternative splicing by interacting with DDX21 in colorectal cancer.
abstract: Truncating mutations in the adenomatous polyposis coli (APC) gene-a key driver of colorectal cancer (CRC) initiation-frequently lead to the production of a truncated APC protein (Trunc-APC). However, its post-transcriptional roles and oncogenic potential remain largely unexplored. Here, we demonstrate that Trunc-APC functions as an RNA-binding protein, directly associating with pre-mRNA via its N-terminal 1-169 amino acid region to regulate widespread alternative splicing (AS) in CRC cells. Specifically, Trunc-APC promotes exon inclusion in ARHGEF11, producing an oncogenic isoform that is associated with enhanced Bcl-xL/BAX complex formation and reduced apoptosis. Mechanistically, Trunc-APC interacts with the RNA helicase DDX21 and facilitates SF3B complex recruitment to pre-mRNA, thereby modulating splicing patterns. Notably, treatment with the splicing inhibitor Madrasin significantly reduced tumor burden in ApcMin/+ CRC mice, indicating strong antitumor efficacy. Collectively, these findings establish Trunc-APC as a novel regulator of alternative splicing and a promoter of CRC progression, and highlight the therapeutic potential of targeting the Trunc-APC/DDX21/SF3B axis in CRC.

title: CircSMOX in muscle and neuronal physiology and disease.
abstract: Circular RNAs (circRNAs) are single stranded RNA molecules with a covalently closed loop structure that confers remarkable stability. They are increasingly recognized as important regulators of gene expression, showing tissue- and stage-specific expression patterns. CircRNAs influence gene expression through several routes: many sequester microRNAs, others bind specific RNA-binding proteins, and some affect transcription or post-transcriptional control. A subset can even be translated into short peptides. They are particularly abundant in the nervous system and in skeletal muscle, where they contribute to processes such as neural development, synaptic function, neuronal plasticity, muscle formation, and tissue homeostasis. Disruptions in circRNA expression patterns have been linked to neurodegenerative conditions, muscle-wasting disorders, and other disease states. Among the known circRNAs, circSMOX-formed from exons 2 and 3 of the murine SMOX gene-has been found dynamically expressed during brain and muscle development and increased in models of ischemia, spinal cord damage, and muscle atrophy. During C2C12 myogenic differentiation, circSMOX expression parallels that of the linear SMOX transcript. In contrast, in dexamethasone-induced atrophy and in ALS mouse models (SOD1G93A and hFUS+/+), which exhibit progressive muscle atrophy, circSMOX is significantly upregulated. Mainly localized in the cytoplasm and less abundant than the linear isoform, circSMOX acts as a miR-340-5p sponge, influencing neuroinflammatory pathways. Despite these insights, the precise molecular mechanisms of circSMOX remain to be fully clarified, and the identification of a human ortholog will be important to broaden its therapeutic potential.

title: Autophagy induction mitigates FUS aggregate formation and early synaptic dysfunction at the NMJ in a FUS-ALS model.
abstract: Mutations in Fused in Sarcoma (FUS), an RNA binding protein, cause Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis (ALS). ALS is an aggressive neurodegenerative disease resulting in motor neuron degeneration. Defects in synaptic integrity precede neuronal loss in ALS, but the mechanisms responsible for these early synaptic defects are unclear. To investigate early synaptic defects associated with ALS, we expressed an ALS-linked variant of human FUS in adult motor neurons and assessed synaptic pathology at the neuromuscular junction (NMJ). Here, we highlight the accumulation of FUS-positive aggregates at synaptic terminals and subsequent reduction in microtubule stability. Autophagy induction via expression of Rab1 or Fragile-X Mental Retardation Protein 1 (FMR1), or treatment with rapamycin reduces aggregate formation and restores synaptic structure and function. These findings reveal the utility of inducing autophagy to address early synaptic dysfunction in an ALS model and demonstrate a potential therapeutic target to preventing later stages of disease progression.Teaser Maintaining synaptic integrity protects motor neurons in a model of ALS.

title: Beyond the membrane: the overlooked nuclear localization of the prion protein.
abstract: Although the prion protein (PrP) is best known as a glycosylphosphatidylinositol-anchored cell surface glycoprotein lacking canonical nucleic acid-binding domains, accumulating evidence indicates that it can be localized in the cytosol and nucleus and exhibits a remarkable ability to interact with both RNA and DNA molecules. A wide range of nucleic acids have been identified as PrP interactors, including cellular and viral RNAs, genomic and mitochondrial DNA, as well as highly structured nucleic acid motifs. For instance, G-quadruplexes and DNA hairpin aptamers, often display particularly high affinity for PrP. These observations suggest that PrP's nucleic acid binding property is a potentially overlooked part of PrP biology, with possible implications for its physiological functions and pathological roles, including the formation of biomolecular condensates. While such condensates might participate in the spatiotemporal organization of PrP biological activities, their aging into less dynamic, gel- or solid-like assemblies could also contribute to pathological protein aggregation linked to prion disease pathogenesis. Herein, we review the literature about nuclear-associated PrP and discuss its molecular features relevant to nucleic-acid binding. Furthermore, we argue that PrP might harbor previously underappreciated nuclear functions as supported by microscopy and biochemical evidence reporting intranuclear and perinuclear PrP. We propose that this understudied nuclear localization of PrP might stem from the historical focus on membrane-associated PrP, and we call for renewed attention to its potential nuclear activities.

title: SnoDB 3.0: a specialized database featuring murine and human annotation and cross-species correspondence for the snoRNA community.
abstract: Small nucleolar RNAs (snoRNAs) are a large, evolutionarily conserved family of non-coding RNAs that guide ribosomal RNA (rRNA) modifications. Recent years have seen growing interest in the biological and biomedical roles of snoRNAs, their guided rRNA modifications, and their alternative functions. snoDB is a specialized database that aggregates human snoRNA annotations and features, including genomic location, host gene, conserved motifs, protein and RNA interactors, expression levels, as well as rRNA target sites and modification levels. In this third release, we expand the database to include murine snoRNAs with an equivalent level of annotation, update human snoRNA host genes, RNA interactors and protein interactors, and introduce new tools to establish snoRNA and rRNA target cross-species correspondence. snoDB 3.0 is available at https://bioinfo-scottgroup.med.usherbrooke.ca/snoDB/.

title: The complete mitochondrial genome and phylogenetic position of Acrocalymma sp. LF1 (Acrocalymmaceae) isolated from blueberry.
abstract: Acrocalymma (Acrocalymmaceae, Dothideomycetes) mitogenomes remain largely uncharacterized, thereby restricting evolutionary analyses of this ecologically significant lineage. We assembled the Acrocalymma sp. LF1 mitogenome using Illumina short-read sequencing data, while performing phylogenetic analyses involving concatenated mitochondrial protein-coding sequences from 28 representative Dothideomycetes species. The assembled circular mitogenome consisted of 34,373 bp (AT content, 71.8%) and included 13 protein-coding genes, two ribosomal RNA genes, and 26 transfer RNA (tRNA) genes. Most protein-coding genes had ATG and TAA as start and stop codons, respectively, but cox1 had an incomplete stop codon (T-). Seven tRNAs had secondary structures that deviated from the canonical cloverleaf model. Additionally, two identical copies of the trnV-TAC tRNA gene were located at two distinct genomic loci. Phylogenetic analyses revealed that Acrocalymma sp. LF1 formed a fully supported sister relationship with Acrocalymma vagum in the family Acrocalymmaceae (bootstrap support = 100%). This study has enriched the mitogenomic dataset of Acrocalymmaceae and provides a fundamental genomic resource for subsequent systematic and evolutionary studies. Moreover, it confirms the utility of mitochondrial genomes for resolving phylogenetic relationships within this fungal lineage.

title: MethMarkerDB 2.0: an expanded and functionally annotated database for cancer DNA methylation biomarkers.
abstract: Cancer-associated differentially methylated regions (DMRs) are promising biomarkers for cancer diagnosis, prognosis, and therapeutic response, but their biological significance and potential applications remain to be systematically explored across datasets. To support this, we released MethMarkerDB 2.0 (https://methmarkerdb.hzau.edu.cn/v2), which provides several improvements over the previous version: (i) Expands the data resource from 13 to 21 cancer types and from 658 to 1236 whole-genome methylome samples, comprising ∼5.6 million candidate DMRs and 6411 literature-curated biomarker records.(ii) Integrates 450K DNA methylation data from The Cancer Genome Atlas and Epigenome-Wide Association Study Atlas and transcript annotations into the "MethMarker Gene Search" module. These data provide complementary evidence from independent datasets and platforms and allow users to examine CpG-level information for individual DMRs. Additionally, cell-type-resolved reference methylation data allow users to check cellular-background methylation. (iii) Introduces four analysis modules to characterize DMR methylation patterns across age groups and spatial ecotypes, and connect DMRs with transcription factor binding evidence and cancer cell-line drug responses. Moreover, the "Methylation-Cas Designer" supports guide RNA design for methylation-sensitive restriction enzyme-Cas assays and targeted epigenome editing. In summary, MethMarkerDB 2.0 provides expanded resources, diverse functional analyses, and experimental design tools, facilitating the interpretation and application of cancer-associated DMRs.

title: Integrated in silico assessment of the regulatory and structural consequences of pulmonary tuberculosis-associated SP110 polymorphisms.
abstract: The molecular mechanisms underlying conflicting findings of association of SP110 single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) with susceptibility to pulmonary tuberculosis (PTB) remain unclear. We selected ten SP110 SNPs from publicly available genomic databases, based on prior PTB association and minor allele frequencies exceeding 1% in African populations and identified in a Ugandan cohort with PTB. We then applied in silico multi-tool framework, incorporating deep-learning splice predictors including SpliceAI, Pangolin, and AlphaGenome, to evaluate the regulatory and functional consequences of the SNPs on transcription factor binding, RNA splicing, RNA secondary structure, and protein-level effects. The model captured population-relevant SP110 variations rather than a directly genotyped Ugandan cohort. Our analysis revealed allele-specific gains and losses involving transcription factors TFAP2A, TFAP2C, TP63, Zfx, and IRF1, suggesting modulation of regulatory potential through altered transcription factor binding motifs. However, SpliceAI and Pangolin uniformly predicted low splice-disruptive effects across both exonic and intronic variants, while multiple protein pathogenicity tools consistently classified missense and stop-gained variants as benign or tolerated. RNA secondary structure analysis predicted that most variants preserved global thermodynamic stability. From our findings, SP110 variants are unlikely to exert major effects through splicing disruption or protein destabilization but may contribute to functional diversity through subtle regulatory mechanisms, including transcription factor binding modulation and RNA structural reorganization. The online version contains supplementary material available at https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-026-65881-y.

title: Quantification of Prime Editor-Corrected Frameshift Mutations Using Bioluminescence Resonance Energy Transfer (BRET).
abstract: Frameshift mutations, caused by insertions or deletions of nucleotides that disrupt the coding reading frame, often result in premature stop codons, terminating protein translation. Prime editing, a precise genome-editing tool, has demonstrated remarkable efficiency in correcting such mutations even in living organisms. Prime editors are fusion proteins that combine a nickase variant of Cas9 (nCas9; H840A), which induces single-strand nicks in double-stranded DNA, with a modified reverse transcriptase. This system uses an extended guide RNA (pegRNA) that includes a primer-binding site and a reverse transcriptase template for the desired edit. Bioluminescence Resonance Energy Transfer (BRET) quantifies molecular interactions via energy transfer from a luminescent donor to a fluorescent acceptor. In this context, BRET is employed to measure the correction of frameshift mutations by restoring acceptor fluorophore expression. The donor luciferase coding sequence, located upstream of the frameshift mutation, remains unaffected and serves as an internal standard, ensuring reliable quantification independently of experimental fluctuations.

title: Design of Highly Efficient pegRNAs with Minimized Off-Target Effects Using DeepPrime.
abstract: Prime editors are newly developed genome editing tools capable of installing various types of mutations without introducing double-strand DNA breaks (DSBs) or requiring donor DNA templates. Prime editors consist of a Cas9 nickase fused to a reverse transcriptase (RT) domain and function as a ribonucleoprotein complex with prime editing guide RNA (pegRNA). Unlike the single guide RNA (sgRNA) used with Cas9 or base editors, the editing efficiency of pegRNAs is determined by the sequence composition and length of the guide sequence, primer binding site (PBS), and reverse transcription template (RTT). The high design flexibility of pegRNAs presents both opportunities and challenges. Therefore, designing pegRNAs with high efficacy has been a significant hurdle for the application of prime editing. Here, we present a step-by-step protocol for designing optimal pegRNAs to introduce desired edits using a deep learning-based algorithm, DeepPrime.

title: pegRNA Online Tool Design and Experimental Assembly: Exploring the Practical Use of PE-Designer for Prime Editing.
abstract: Prime editing (PE) is an innovative genome-editing technology that enables precise genetic modifications with greater efficiency compared to traditional CRISPR/Cas9-based systems. The successful application of this method heavily depends on the design of prime editing guide RNAs (pegRNAs). Efficient design of pegRNAs is facilitated by online tools like PE-Designer ( www.rgenome.net/pe-designer/) , which offers a user-friendly interface for designing pegRNA and nicking single-guide RNA (sgRNA) sequences. Notable features of PE-Designer include its flexibility in adjusting the prime binding site (PBS) and reverse transcription template (RTT) lengths of pegRNAs, as well as its ability to assess potential off-target effects across various genomes. This chapter focuses on using PE-Designer for pegRNA design, providing a step-by-step guide to the tool while addressing frequent challenges. Furthermore, using the SnapGene software, we explore the assembly of both the pegRNA and sgRNA construct maps. Finally, the chapter presents the experimental protocol for constructing both the pegRNA and sgRNA vectors, with a detailed explanation of the Golden Gate assembly technique.

title: A sequence-encoded promoter-proximal super pause stabilizes an offline RNA polymerase II state.
abstract: Promoter-proximal pausing by RNA polymerase II is critical for regulating gene expression in multicellular eukaryotes. How nucleic acid sequence and protein factors contribute to pausing remains incompletely understood. We developed gene-specific analysis of transcriptional output (GATO)-seq, which enables massively parallel, temporally resolved, reconstituted transcription in an assay that uses direct RNA sequencing to map 3' ends of nascent transcripts from a library of human genes. GATO-seq identified a "super pause" sequence that potently induces RNA polymerase II pausing and is not relieved by transcription factor (TF) IIS. Cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) structures of RNA polymerase II on the super-pause sequence revealed a previously unobserved, reversible single-nucleotide backtracked state ("sidetracked"), stabilized by a threonine-lined pocket that limits further backtracking. Together, we introduce a powerful in vitro technique to study transcription regulation and show that nucleic acid sequence encodes pausing propensity and traps sequence-specific offline states, linking sequence to pausing control.

title: [The impact of Cirbp knockout on the expression of immune-related genes in the cortex of developing mice].
abstract: Objective To investigate how cold-inducible RNA-binding protein (Cirbp) knockout affects the expression of immune-related genes in the cerebral cortex during postnatal development. Methods Wild-type (WT) and Cirbp knockout (Cirbp-) C57BL/6 mice were euthanized at postnatal day 21 (P21), and cortical tissues were collected. Western blot was used to detect CIRBP protein expression in cortical tissues. Transcriptome sequencing was performed to identify differentially expressed genes (DEGs), thereby facilitating the identification of key immune-related genes. Candidate genes were validated using real-time quantitative PCR. Results Western blot confirmed the absence of CIRBP protein expression in the cortex of Cirbp- mice. Compared with the WT group, transcriptomic analysis identified 268 DEGs in the cortex of Cirbp- mice, of which 118 were upregulated and 150 were downregulated. Gene Ontology (GO) enrichment analysis showed that the DEGs were mainly enriched in biological processes including signal transduction, transmembrane transport, and positive regulation of transcription by RNA polymerase II. Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) pathway enrichment analysis indicated that the DEGs were predominantly enriched in the cytosolic DNA-sensing pathway, tumor necrosis factor (TNF) signaling pathway, and Toll-like receptor signaling pathway. REACTOME pathway enrichment revealed that the DEGs were mainly enriched in signal transduction, peptide ligand-binding receptors, and downstream signaling pathways of G protein-coupled receptors. In the protein-protein interaction (PPI) network, the identified immune-related genes in the cortex included interleukin 6 (IL-6), C-C motif chemokine ligand 4 (CCL4), CCL5, C-X-C motif chemokine ligand 10 (CXCL10), cellular communication network factor 1(CCN1), and cluster of Differentiation 274 (CD274). Real-time quantitative PCR validation showed that the mRNA expression levels of these key immune-related genes were consistent with the RNA sequencing results. Conclusion Cirbp knockout significantly alters the expression of immune-related genes in the cortex of developing mice, providing candidate targets for subsequent investigations into the protein-level underlying CIRBP-mediated neuroimmune regulation.

title: Microbiome evidence-guided construction of a defined microbial consortium for light-aroma Baijiu fermentation and flavor development.
abstract: Natural fermentation systems harbor microbial resources, but translating microbiome information into cultivable and controllable defined communities remains challenging. We integrated 74 metagenomic datasets from light-aroma Baijiu-associated Daqu and fermented grains with metagenome-assembled genome (MAG) functional profiles and independent 16S ribosomal RNA (rRNA) gene and internal transcribed spacer (ITS) amplicon time series to propose four candidate functional roles: substrate conversion, acid/acyl-precursor formation, alcoholic fermentation, and aroma formation. Metagenomic profiling revealed community heterogeneity, whereas MAG analysis showed widespread genetic potential for starch conversion and lactic- and acetic-acid-related metabolism. Amplicon data revealed genus-level temporal distributions of Bacillus, Weissella, Wickerhamomyces, and Saccharomyces. Bacillus amyloliquefaciens, Weissella confusa, Saccharomyces cerevisiae, and Wickerhamomyces anomalus were selected from the available laboratory culture collection as candidate representatives of these roles. A three-factor Box-Behnken design optimized the two bacterial inoculum volumes and the combined yeast volume, with the yeast ratio fixed at 1:1 (v/v). For 500 g of substrate, inoculation volumes were 7 mL for B. amyloliquefaciens, 20 mL for W. confusa, 41 mL for S. cerevisiae, and 41 mL for W. anomalus, yielding 2.28 ± 0.12 g/L ethyl acetate (HPLC). During 28 d of solid-state fermentation, starch, reducing sugars, acidity, and volatile profiles changed, with 51 volatile compounds detected. The final base Baijiu contained 33 volatile compounds, including 13 with odor activity values (OAVs) >1, of which 11 were also detected by gas chromatography-olfactometry (GC-O). These findings support a role-guided route from natural fermentation microbiome evidence to a defined consortium with measurable fermentation and flavor phenotypes.

title: Nuclear retention and RNA editing safeguard self-tolerance to immunogenic intron lariats
abstract: Introns are excised as lariats and rapidly degraded upon linearization, leaving their post-splicing role unclear. Here, we investigate their immunoregulatory potential by analyzing the intron lariat landscape upon inhibition of the debranching enzyme DBR1. We find that lariats harboring transposable elements (TEs), especially inverted Alu repeats (IRAlus), elicit cell cycle-dependent activation of protein kinase R (PKR), but only in cells harboring a high burden, such as breast cancer. These immunogenic lariats are initially retained in the nucleus, but upon cytosolic release, they drive PKR activation and apoptosis. Exploiting this, we combine DBR1 depletion with anti-mitotic chemotherapy to enhance lariat-PKR interactions and promote cancer cell death in vitro and in vivo. We further show that A-to-I editing of IRAlus-containing lariats weakens their interaction with PKR and suppresses PKR activation. Our findings highlight two parallel molecular mechanisms to sustain self-tolerance to repeat-rich introns, revealing a vulnerability exploitable for anti-tumor therapy.

title: Alcohol exposure induces reversible nucleolar amyloidogenesis.
abstract: The nucleolus is a dynamic membraneless organelle that rapidly responds to cellular perturbations. Under harsh environmental conditions, it transitions from a ribosome biogenesis center into a dense proteinaceous structure, known as a nucleolar amyloid body (A-body). Although A-bodies share biophysical characteristics with pathological amyloids, these physiological structures are non-toxic, protective, and reversible. Here, we identify alcohol exposure as an A-body-inducing stimulus. Our findings demonstrate that cells remain viable during alcohol treatment and that ethanol-induced A-bodies are reversible upon restoration of physiological conditions. These structures form through a signaling pathway distinct from previously characterized stimuli, yet still require the proto-oncogene c-Myc and regulatory noncoding RNAs to drive nucleolar remodeling. Ethanol also induces a distinct A-body proteome, allowing us to investigate how protein structure governs selective susceptibility to different denaturing environments. Using homologous RNA helicases, we demonstrate that single amino acid substitutions can dramatically alter stress-dependent protein destabilization and recruitment to A-bodies. Similarly, disease-associated protein variants display altered aggregation behavior relative to their wild-type counterparts. Together, this work establishes alcohol exposure as a physiological trigger of reversible nucleolar amyloid formation and provides insight into how protein structure may have evolved to influence susceptibility to stress-induced misfolding. The online version contains supplementary material available at https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-026-66031-0.

title: Host CD59 potentiates the type III secretion system in Yersinia pseudotuberculosis.
abstract: Type III secretion systems (T3SS) play critical roles in disease for many Gram-negative pathogens. Although the structural details of T3SS assembly have been extensively studied, the intimate interactions between T3SS components and the target host plasma membrane are poorly characterized. A previous RNA interference (RNAi) study identified the GPI-linked surface protein CD59 as a critical host component that supports the translocation of Yersinia pseudotuberculosis (Yptb) T3SS effectors into the host cytosol. We show here that both depletion and increased levels of CD59 reduced Yptb T3SS pore formation and Yop translocation into host target cells. CD59 is unlikely to act as a receptor for the T3SS translocon, as physical blockade of CD59 or enzymatic removal of all GPI-linked surface proteins had no effect on T3SS function. Consistent with its importance in supporting T3SS function, efficient bacterial effector-mediated focal adhesion disassembly was dependent on CD59. Surprisingly, depletion of CD59 interfered with the rearrangement of the lipid raft marker GM1 that occurs after Yptb adhesion to host cells, indicating that CD59 supports lipid microdomain dynamics. Consistent with a role in modulating lipid composition, the loss of CD59 led to the accumulation of phosphatidylcholine and alterations in both fatty acid chain lengths and saturation levels. This work points to a role for CD59 in maintaining plasma membrane dynamics necessary for efficient T3SS translocon function. In addition, a polarization index is described that quantifies the asymmetric association of membrane compartments with organelles. The online version contains supplementary material available at https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-026-65480-x.

title: The tRNA methylation activity and specificity of NSUN2 are independent of Archease.
abstract: Transfer RNAs (tRNAs) undergo extensive maturation, including modifications essential for translation efficiency and fidelity, as well as for structural stability. The modification cytosine-5 methylation (m5C) is catalyzed by NSUN2 at multiple positions within distinct structural regions of a subset of tRNAs, yet the determinants of its substrate specificity remain elusive. In archaea, the protein Archease has been implicated in modulating the cytosine specificity of the NSUN2 ortholog Trm4, whereas mammalian Archease was shown to be involved in pre-tRNA splicing. Here, we investigated whether mammalian Archease influences NSUN2 in a similar way like the archaeal enzyme. Using short hairpin RNA-mediated depletion of Archease in mouse embryonic stem cells and in vitro methylation assays with recombinant proteins, we assessed both the catalytic activity and substrate selectivity of NSUN2 in the presence or the absence of Archease. Our results indicate that neither the efficiency nor positional specificity of NSUN2-mediated tRNA m5C methylation is affected by Archease. These findings indicate that, unlike in archaea, Archease does not regulate tRNA methylation by NSUN2 in mammals, highlighting an evolutionary divergence in the functional role of Archease in tRNA maturation pathways. The online version contains supplementary material available at https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-026-63726-2.

title: A novel partitivirus induces hypovirulence and increases pyraclostrobin sensitivity in the phytopathogenic fungus Lasiodiplodia ziziphi.
abstract: Lasiodiplodia ziziphi causes canker disease in jujube and other woody plants. Its control relies mainly on fungicides. Mycoviruses that cause hypovirulence are an emerging option for the biological control of fungal diseases. In this study, we identified a novel double-stranded RNA (dsRNA) mycovirus, Lasiodiplodia ziziphi partitivirus 1 (LzPV1), from L. ziziphi strain CDZM004. The LzPV1 genome consists of two dsRNA segments. dsRNA1 (1,905 bp) encodes an RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (RdRp), and dsRNA2 (1,773 bp) encodes a capsid protein (CP). The genome is packaged into isometric virions about 32 nm in diameter. Phylogenetic analysis of the RdRp and CP placed LzPV1 in the genus Alphapartitivirus of the family Partitiviridae. LzPV1 was transmitted horizontally through hyphal anastomosis and vertically through conidia. LzPV1 infection reduced the virulence of L. ziziphi, changed its hyphal morphology, and increased fungal sensitivity to the fungicide pyraclostrobin. This is the first mycovirus reported in L. ziziphi and the first partitivirus described in the genus Lasiodiplodia. LzPV1 is a promising biocontrol resource for jujube canker disease.

title: Structure-Based Design of 2-(Pyridone)Indoles as Antagonists of the Toll-Like Receptors TLR7 and TLR8 for the Treatment of Autoimmune Disorders.
abstract: Toll-like receptors 7 and 8 (TLR7/8) are innate immune sensors whose activation by endogenous RNA ligands is a hallmark of chronic autoimmune disorders, notably cutaneous and systemic lupus. We present the structure-based design and optimization of 2-(pyridin-2(1H)-one)indoles as potent dual TLR7/8 antagonists with properties improved over our prior series, including increased permeability, reduced ion channel activity, and reduced volume of distribution at steady state (Vss). Initial pyridone leads displayed unexpected anti-proliferative activity in a panel of immune cell lines; optimization against an identified off-target BRD4 liability, hypothesized to drive this effect, delivered potent antagonists devoid of BRD4 binding and of anti-proliferative activity. These compounds potently inhibited TLR7/8-mediated IL-6 production in human whole blood, with 9a giving IC50 values of 9.4 and 1.3 nM against TLR7 and TLR8, respectively. This orally bioavailable lead dose-dependently suppressed TLR7-mediated IL-6 and IFNα release in a mouse pharmacodynamic model.

title: Hepatitis C, Hearing Loss, and Healthcare Utilization Patterns, a Cross-Sectional Analysis of NHANES Data: 1999-2012.
abstract: Hearing loss is a chronic condition in the U.S. with diverse causes, including viral infections, and significantly affects quality of life. Despite the rising incidence of Hepatitis C virus (HCV) infection, research on its relationship with hearing loss remains limited. Early and consistent interactions with the healthcare system have been shown to improve outcomes in extrahepatic manifestations of HCV and enhance quality of life. We conducted a cross-sectional analysis of HCV history, identified via HCV antibody and RNA testing obtained by the mobile examination center, and hearing loss, measured by pure-tone audiometry, using National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey data (1999-2004, 2011-2012) for adults aged 20 to 69. We utilized multivariable logistic regression models to estimate odds ratios (ORs) and 95% confidence intervals, adjusting for important covariates. Results were stratified by degree of healthcare utilization. Among 6705 participants, hearing loss prevalence was 27.7% in those with HCV versus 12.7% in those without. The adjusted OR for hearing loss in individuals with HCV was 1.81 (95% confidence interval: 1.06, 3.10). Notably, the magnitude of association between HCV history and hearing loss was higher in the low healthcare utilization group than in the high healthcare utilization group (aOR: 2.82 versus 0.72). Our findings suggest an association between HCV and hearing loss, with healthcare utilization modifying this relationship. This study fills a gap in the literature and highlights the need for increased clinical monitoring of hearing health in individuals who have had an HCV infection.

title: m6A coordinates mumps virus replication and innate immune sensing.
abstract: In this study, we test the hypothesis that N6-methyladenosine (m6A) coordinates a functional trade-off between viral replication and innate immune sensing during mumps virus (MuV) infection. Using single-base resolution GLORI-seq, we identified widespread and non-canonically distributed m6A sites across MuV genomic, antigenomic, and messenger RNAs. Functional analyses revealed that depletion of the m6A methyltransferase METTL3 enhances viral RNA synthesis and nucleocapsid encapsidation in interferon-deficient cells, indicating an intrinsic suppressive role of m6A in viral replication. In contrast, in immune-competent epithelial and dendritic cells, host m6A enhances antiviral signaling, as METTL3 deficiency reduces infection-induced interferon and cytokine responses. Mechanistically, m6A-deficient MuV RNA exhibited increased binding to multiple pattern recognition receptors, including RIG-I-like and toll-like receptors, resulting in enhanced innate immune activation. Additionally, MuV infection extensively remodels the host m6A epitranscriptome in a cell type-dependent manner, with m6A enrichment positively correlating with the expression of immune-related transcripts. Together, these findings demonstrate that m6A acts as a bidirectional regulator during MuV infection by simultaneously restricting viral replication and modulating host immune recognition, providing new insight into epitranscriptomic control of paramyxovirus-host interactions.IMPORTANCEN6-methyladenosine (m6A) modification has emerged as a key regulator of RNA virus infection, yet its role in mumps virus (MuV) remains undefined. Here, we map the single-base resolution m6A landscape of a recombinant MuV and demonstrate that viral m6A restricts genome encapsidation and replication while attenuating innate immune sensing. MuV infection extensively remodels host m6A profiles in epithelial and dendritic cells, preferentially enhancing methylation of innate immune transcripts. Strikingly, m6A-deficient MuV RNA exhibits increased affinity for RIG-I-like and toll-like receptors, eliciting stronger interferon and proinflammatory responses. Our findings identify m6A as a bidirectional regulator of MuV replication and immunity and suggest an epitranscriptomic strategy to optimize live-attenuated vaccine design.

title: Phosphoregulation of RNAPII transcription from initiation to pausing to termination.
abstract: Transcription by eukaryotic RNA polymerase II (RNAPII) is regulated both before and after initiation. A prime example of post-initiation control is the promoter-proximal pause, which ensures complete assembly of RNAPII elongation complexes and proper processing of the nascent transcript. Satisfaction of this checkpoint is a step toward production of mature, full-length mRNA, whereas failure to do so can lead to promoter-proximal transcript termination or RNAPII degradation. Both pause establishment and release are regulated by reversible protein phosphorylation. Cyclin-dependent kinase (CDK) 7, associated with initiation factor TFIIH, phosphorylates RNAPII to enable its escape from the promoter and assembly into a paused complex with the DRB sensitivity-inducing factor (DSIF) and Negative Elongation Factor (NELF), while CDK9, the catalytic subunit of positive transcription elongation factor b (P-TEFb), phosphorylates RNAPII, the SPT5 subunit of DSIF, NELF and possibly other proteins to overcome this block to elongation. Multisite phosphorylation of SPT5 by CDK9 times pause release, regulates elongation speed and coordinates transcription with RNA processing. Pause release and processive elongation are favored by phosphorylation of the RNA-binding loop of SPT5, and opposed by protein phosphatase 4 (PP4) and Integrator-associated protein phosphatase 2A (PP2A), while the stimulatory effects of SPT5 carboxy-terminal phosphorylation on elongation rate are reversed by protein phosphatase 1 (PP1) to facilitate termination. In this review, we summarize the current understanding of the kinase-phosphatase interplay that coordinates steps of the RNAPII transcription cycle to ensure productive mRNA synthesis and cell viability, with a focus on the tripartite phosphorylation of SPT5.

title: Advances in siRNA delivery for breast cancer therapy: from molecular design to therapeutic application.
abstract: Breast cancer progression is driven by molecular heterogeneity, drug resistance (DR), and interactions within the tumour microenvironment (TME), creating an urgent need for therapies that can selectively suppress disease-associated genes. Small interfering RNA (siRNA) can silence targets involved in tumour growth, treatment resistance, and immune evasion. Its therapeutic potential, however, depends on overcoming rapid degradation and clearance, limited tumour accumulation, poor cellular uptake, and endosomal entrapment. Lipid-based and polymer-mediated delivery systems (DS) protect siRNA and facilitate its transport, while chemical modifications, molecular conjugates, and physical delivery methods offer additional ways to improve stability or access to target cells. In BC models, these strategies have been investigated for targeted therapy, reversal of DR, and modulation of the TME to support antitumor immunity. Despite encouraging preclinical findings, effective tumour delivery, sustained gene silencing, off-target effects, and immune activation remain significant barriers to clinical translation. This review brings together advances in siRNA delivery and their applications against BC progression, DR, and immune evasion, while defining the barriers that must be overcome to translate effective gene silencing into meaningful clinical benefit.

title: Survey of viruses associated with the whitefly Bemisia tabaci in cucurbits in Georgia, United States.
abstract: Whiteflies (Bemisia tabaci) are major agricultural pests causing over $100 million in losses to vegetable production annually through the transmission of plant viruses. Characterizing the virome of B. tabaci is critical for understanding vectoring potential and identifying candidate viral biocontrol agents. In this study, B. tabaci were collected from cucurbit crops in Tifton, Georgia, across two consecutive years, 2023 and 2024. Total RNA was extracted and ribodepleted, then sequenced with 150 bp paired-end reads on the Illumina NovaSeq 6000. Bioinformatics analyses included quality-assessing raw reads, which were trimmed prior to mapping to the B. tabaci reference genome (GCF_918797505.1) on the Alabama HPC, then mapping to a viral database (viral2019-03) using the Galaxy platform. After de novo transcriptome assembly using rnaviralSPAdes, the assembled contigs were screened for viral similarity using BLAST-based searches against the NCBI non-redundant nucleotide (nt) and non-redundant protein (nr) databases. Candidate viral contigs were evaluated by read mapping, coverage assessment, taxonomic assignment, and open reading frame prediction. The analysis identified contigs representing plant, bacteriophage, and insect-associated viruses. Near-complete cucurbit chlorotic yellows virus (CCYV) RNA1 and RNA2 sequences were assembled from both years, with higher abundance in 2024. A dicistrovirus-like sequence related to Cripavirus was also detected in both years and contained both major open reading frames. CCYV and the dicistrovirus-like sequence were the only viral targets with sufficient read support for genome assembly and molecular validation in both sampling years.

title: Cloning and molecular characterization of an ovine ABCD4 cDNA sequence, recombinant protein expression, and polyclonal antibody generation in Ujimqin sheep.
abstract: ATP-binding cassette subfamily D member 4 (ABCD4) is an ATP-binding cassette transporter involved in intracellular cobalamin trafficking and has also been identified as a candidate gene associated with vertebral-number variation in livestock. However, molecular information and experimental resources for ovine ABCD4 remain limited. This study aimed to characterize a RACE-derived ABCD4 cDNA sequence from Ujimqin sheep, analyze its sequence and predicted molecular features, establish a recombinant protein expression system, and generate a polyclonal antibody resource for subsequent studies. Total RNA isolated from Ujimqin sheep liver was subjected to rapid amplification of cDNA ends (RACE), followed by sequence analysis, phylogenetic comparison, physicochemical characterization, recombinant expression in Escherichia coli, protein purification, and antibody production. A 1,874-bp ABCD4 cDNA sequence was obtained, containing a predicted 1,209-bp open reading frame encoding a 402-amino-acid polypeptide. Sequence and bioinformatic analyses showed that the RACE-derived sequence retained conserved features of the ABC transporter family, although its predicted protein length was shorter than that of canonical mammalian ABCD4 proteins. For recombinant antigen production, the ABCD4 expression construct was introduced into E. coli BL21 (DE3), and higher recombinant protein expression was observed after induction with 0.5 mM IPTG at 37 °C for 4 h. The recombinant protein was predominantly recovered from the insoluble fraction and purified by Ni-NTA affinity chromatography. Purified recombinant protein was then used to immunize New Zealand White rabbits solely for polyclonal antiserum production, and the resulting antisera showed strong immunoreactivity against the recombinant antigen. Overall, this study provides a RACE-derived ovine ABCD4 cDNA sequence together with recombinant protein and antibody resources that may support future investigations of ABCD4 expression, localization, and biological function in sheep.

title: Expanding the Phenotypic Spectrum of FTO-Related Developmental Disorder Caused by Biallelic Variants in FTO.
abstract: Fat Mass and Obesity-Associated (FTO) gene encodes a versatile RNA-modifying enzyme that regulates gene expression, RNA processing, and protein synthesis by demethylating different RNA substrates. FTO has a wide range of effects on mammalian physiological functions in regulating fat mass, adipogenesis, and energy homeostasis. Bi-allelic variants in FTO cause growth failure, developmental delay, and facial dysmorphism. Earlier reported individuals carried variants at critical catalytic sites and had severe developmental phenotypes with early childhood lethality. We report 13 additional individuals from nine families with variable prenatal and postnatal phenotypes with variants in FTO (NM_001080432.3). We add a presumably founder variant c.608 T>C in seven individuals from four Indian families with milder clinical and neuroimaging findings compared to earlier reports. We reviewed genotype-phenotypes of the current series and previous individuals with FTO-related developmental disorders. We also document the prenatal phenotypes of FTO variants, thereby expanding the spectrum of FTO-related developmental anomalies.

title: Emerging Technologies for Viability Assessment of Foodborne Pathogens: From Molecular Dyes to Artificial Intelligence.
abstract: To critically examine emerging technologies for assessing foodborne-pathogen viability and to evaluate their relevance for improving food safety monitoring and public-health risk assessment. This review examines the literature on viability-detection using biological indicators such as membrane integrity, infectivity, and virulence. It addresses technologies such as viability dye-based PCR, RNA and CRISPR detection methods, biosensors, bacteriophage assays, Raman spectroscopy, and AI-supported analysis. Compared to conventional culture-based and DNA-only molecular methods, viability-focused techniques support more biologically meaningful detection, particularly for viable but non-culturable (VBNC) cells that may retain pathogenic potential. However, assay performance varies depending on food-matrix complexity, the presence of inhibitors, sensitivity limitations, and the degree of validation. Integrated systems combining multi-modal sensing, microfluidics, and machine learning have shown increasing promise for rapid on-site application, although standardization and regulatory validation remain limited. The emerging viability-focused technologies substantially refine microbial-risk assessment by accurately capturing the infectious potential of foodborne pathogens, including traditionally undetected VBNC populations. Nevertheless, integrating these technologies into routine surveillance remains constrained by matrix interference and the absence of standardized protocols. Future efforts must prioritize developing matrix-resilient methodologies and establishing regulatory validation frameworks to facilitate their practical implementation in food safety management.

title: Engineering SIM-1 and MZ-1 PROTACs for enhanced target degradation in KSHV-infected immortalized endothelial cells.
abstract: Kaposi's Sarcoma-associated Herpesvirus (KSHV) is the etiologic agent of several human cancers, including Kaposi's Sarcoma (KS), which are still lacking of treatment options. Members of the bromodomain and extra-terminal domain (BET) family, especially bromodomain-containing protein 4 (BRD4), play important roles in RNA polymerase II-mediated transcriptional regulation and are required for the expression of many tumor-driving oncogenes in various cancer cells. Therefore, BET proteins have become attractive targets for anticancer drug development. Our recent studies showed that KSHV-infected immortalized endothelial cells displayed strong resistance to BET inhibitors such as (+)-JQ1. In contrast, we found out MZ-1 and SIM-1, two of BRD4 PROTAC degraders, as effective inhibitors of cell growth in these cells. To develop PROTAC molecules with enhanced BRD4 degradation potency, we introduced an (S)-methyl group at the benzylic position of the VHL ligand in the VHL-based BRD4 PROTACs MZ-1 and SIM-1, thereby designing and generating MZ-1-ME and SIM-1-ME, respectively. In KS cellular model, MZ-1-ME and SIM-1-ME exhibited enhanced BRD4 degradation and anticancer activities compared with their parental compounds, which may represent promising PROTACs for development of BRD4-targeted therapies against KS.

title: Complete mitochondrial genome assembly and comparative analysis of the endangered species Petrocosmea qinlingensis.
abstract: Petrocosmea qinlingensis W. T. Wang (Gesneriaceae) is an endemic species from the Qinling Mountains of China. This species has a restricted distribution and a small population size and has been designated as a National Grade II Protected Plant in China. It has attracted taxonomic and horticultural interest. Although the chloroplast genome of P. qinlingensis has been reported, its mitochondrial genome has not yet been characterized, which limited comparative analyses of mitochondrial genome organization. In this study, we sequenced and assembled the complete mitochondrial genome of P. qinlingensis. The mitogenome of P. qinlingensis is 373,687 bp in length and consists of three circular chromosomes, with an overall GC content of 44.11%. It encodes 35 protein-coding genes, 24 tRNA genes, three rRNA genes, and one pseudogene. A total of 79 SSRs, eight tandem repeats and 124 dispersed repeats were identified. Thirty-one plastid-derived fragments were detected, accounting for 5.24% of the mitochondrial genome. In addition, 535 C-to-U RNA editing sites were predicted across protein-coding genes. Most mitochondrial genes were inferred to be under purifying selection, while several genes showed elevated Ka/Ks ratios. Comparative synteny analyses revealed extensive structural rearrangements among Lamiales mitogenomes. Phylogenetic analysis based on mitochondrial genome data supported the placement of P. qinlingensis within the Gesneriaceae family. This study reported the mitochondrial genome sequence of P. qinlingensis, providing a genomic resource for future comparative and evolutionary studies within Gesneriaceae.

title: Using Prime Editing Guide Generator (PEGG) for High-Throughput Generation of Prime Editing Sensor Libraries.
abstract: Prime editing enables the generation of nearly any small genetic variant. However, the process of prime editing guide RNA (pegRNA) design is challenging and requires automated computational design tools. We developed Prime Editing Guide Generator (PEGG), a fast, flexible, and user-friendly Python package that enables the rapid generation of pegRNA and pegRNA-sensor libraries. Here, we describe the installation and use of PEGG ( https://pegg.readthedocs.io ) to rapidly generate custom pegRNA-sensor libraries for use in high-throughput prime editing screens.

title: Prime Editing: Mechanism and Developments.
abstract: Prime editing is a "search and replace" based genome editing method that can introduce point mutations, insertions, and deletions into DNA at desired sites, making it the editing technique capable of making the most diverse range of edits. Prime editing utilizes a Cas9 nickase fused to a reverse transcriptase to introduce edits encoded by a specially designed DNA oligonucleotide called a prime editing guide RNA (pegRNA). While prime editing has been shown to achieve robust editing in different genomic loci and in different cell types, this technology still has the potential for further optimization and improvement. Many groups have been successful in improving prime editing outcomes by optimizing the design of prime editors and pegRNAs. Additionally, modulating key cellular pathways has also been an effective tool for achieving high levels of editing. Due to its high efficiency and relative safety, prime editing has the potential to transform disease modeling and genomic medicine.

title: From nuclear discovery to organelle-wide regulation: protein lactylation in cancer.
abstract: Protein lysine lactylation is a post-translational modification that links lactate metabolism to the regulation of gene expression and protein function, thereby driving cancer phenotypes. Here, we review current evidence on lactylation through a compartment-specific lens, summarizing its known writers, readers, and erasers, and integrating reported lactylation events across the nucleus, cytoplasm, mitochondria, and cell membrane. In the nucleus, lactylation occurs on both histones and non-histone proteins. Histone lactylation increases chromatin accessibility at active promoters and enhancers to promote transcription, while non-histone protein lactylation regulates gene expression at pre-transcriptional, transcriptional, and post-transcriptional levels, including RNA processing and stability. In the cytoplasm, lactylation influences protein stability, complex assembly, and signaling, with downstream effects on translation. In mitochondria, lactylation intersects with oxidative metabolism, redox homeostasis, and cell-death decisions. At the cell membrane, it modulates lactate transport, receptor signaling, and immune recognition, with consequences for the tumor microenvironment and immune evasion. Finally, we discuss key mechanistic unknowns and therapeutic opportunities arising from this spatially resolved view of lactylation.

title: Arginine kinase is required for successful reproduction in the tick Ixodes ricinus.
abstract: Ticks survive prolonged starvation punctuated by rapid blood feeding and reproduction, imposing substantial changes in metabolic demand. Here, we provide the first functional characterization of arginine kinase from the hard tick Ixodes ricinus (IrAK), an invertebrate phosphagen kinase homologous to vertebrate creatine kinase. IrAK was highly enriched in the midgut, increased following hatching and molting, and reached maximal expression immediately before rapid engorgement. RNAi-mediated silencing of IrAK did not prevent successful blood feeding, significantly affect engorgement weight, or impair nymphal molting, but caused a severe reproductive phenotype characterized by reduced egg production, malformed eggs, and failure to produce viable larvae. Targeted semi-quantitative metabolomic analysis showed that phospho-L-arginine was detected in control midguts of partially fed females but not after IrAK silencing, supporting disruption of the midgut phosphoarginine system. Comparative proteomic analysis of eggs from IrAK-silenced females revealed altered abundance of proteins associated with energy metabolism, cytoskeletal organization, protein turnover, intracellular trafficking, and developmental processes. Although vaccination with recombinant IrAK prolonged tick feeding, it had only limited effects on reproduction. Together, our findings demonstrate an important role for IrAK in successful tick reproduction and identify this vertebrate-absent enzyme as a potential target for further investigation in tick-control strategies.

title: Update on XBP1 in liver pathobiology.
abstract: Chronic liver disease is a major cause of global morbidity and mortality, yet disease-modifying therapies remain scarce. A shared mechanism uniting metabolic, alcohol-associated, viral, drug-induced, cholestatic, and genetic liver injury is endoplasmic reticulum stress and activation of the unfolded protein response. The transcription factor X-box binding protein 1-spliced, a principal output of the inositol-requiring enzyme 1α arm of this response, has emerged as a central determinant of disease pathogenesis. Under endoplasmic reticulum stress, inositol-requiring enzyme 1α splices X-box binding protein 1 messenger RNA to generate the spliced protein, which increases protein folding and degradation capacity and governs hepatic lipogenesis and lipoprotein assembly. A defining feature, however, is its functional dichotomy: typically cytoprotective in hepatocytes but pathogenic in macrophages and stellate cells, and adaptive during transient but maladaptive during unresolved or excessive stress. This dichotomy sans the spectrum of liver diseases and explains, in part, why global manipulation of the pathway has yielded conflicting results and has obstructed targeted drug development. In conclusion, cell-type selectivity is the central translational challenge, preserving protective hepatocyte signaling while restraining it in non-parenchymal cells, which may be addressed through targeted delivery of pharmacologic or genetic therapeutics directed at this pathway in animal models and humans.

title: Defining the druggability of viral macrodomains in coronaviruses and alphaviruses.
abstract: Viral macrodomains are ADP-ribosylhydrolases encoded within the nonstructural proteins of coronaviruses and alphaviruses-2 RNA virus families with pandemic potential. Genetic studies demonstrate that ADP-ribose binding and ADP-ribosylhydrolase activity are critical for replication in alphaviruses and select coronaviruses, such as Middle East respiratory syndrome coronavirus and murine hepatitis virus. In contrast, for severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus (SARS-CoV) and SARS-CoV-2, this domain primarily enhances in vivo fitness by modulating the innate immune response, establishing the macrodomain as a validated antiviral target. Structure-guided and high-throughput efforts have identified selective inhibitors for SARS-CoV-2 and, more recently, early-stage inhibitors of the alphavirus chikungunya virus. Both exploit a conserved active-site architecture that organizes ligand recognition into adenine, phosphate, ribose, and oxyanion subsites. Despite screening of extensive chemical libraries, inhibitor discovery has repeatedly converged on adenine-anchored scaffolds requiring polar engagement of the oxyanion region to achieve potency. This convergence defines a structurally confined druggable corridor but reveals a persistent permeability-potency tradeoff imposed by the polarity required for catalytic engagement. Cross-family comparisons further demonstrate localized divergence that shapes selectivity and constrains straightforward scaffold portability. Here, we synthesize structural, biochemical, and antiviral advances across SARS-CoV-2 and chikungunya virus, define the current boundaries of macrodomain chemical space, and delineate the chemical and biological constraints that now govern translation of catalytic inhibition into predictable antiviral efficacy. SIGNIFICANCE STATEMENT: Viral macrodomains have emerged as compelling antiviral targets in 2 pandemic-potential virus families, coronaviruses and alphaviruses, owing to their conservation and role in virulence. This review defines the chemical space and druggability of the severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 and chikungunya virus macrodomains and the structural and biological constraints that must be overcome to translate catalytic inhibition into next-generation antivirals.

title: Genetic diversity of bacterial endophytes associated with Crotalaria (Rattlepods).
abstract: Crotalaria is a diverse legume genus valued for its ecological and agronomic roles. However, its associated endophytic microbiome remains minimally characterized. This study examined the genetic diversity and community structure of bacterial endophytes inhabiting domesticated and wild Crotalaria species. Twenty-nine healthy Crotalaria plant samples were analyzed using the culture-independent 16S rRNA gene amplicon sequencing approach. Genomic DNA was extracted using the Phenol-Chloroform method from both domesticated and wild samples. Sequencing of 16S ribosomal RNA gene was performed using Illumina MiSeq to profile endophytic bacterial communities. The sequence data was imported into R and processed using Divisive Amplicon Denoising Algorithm 2 (DADA2) pipeline. In total, 1,546,153 high-quality sequence reads were obtained and grouped into 611 amplicon sequence variants (ASVs) at 97% sequence similarity threshold. Domesticated samples exhibited higher observed species richness (median of 39 ASVs) than wild samples (median of 36 ASVs), while wild samples showed greater microbial community evenness (median ~1.08) compared to domesticated samples (median ~0.93). Beta diversity analyses showed clear separation between domesticated and wild endophytic bacterial communities, with domestication status explaining most of the observed variations (PERMANOVA: Bray-Curtis R2 = 0.826; Jaccard R2 = 0.846), but PERMANOVA detected no statistically significant difference (Bray-Curtis and Jaccard; p = 0.067). Overall, five bacteria phyla were detected in the Crotalaria samples. Pseudomonadota was the dominant phylum (64.27%) followed by Cyanobacteriota (35.5%). Enterobacteriaceae was the most abundant family (81.06%) with Enterobacter emerging as the most abundant genus in both domesticated (38.3%) and wild (89.4%) accessions. Notably, Pseudomonas was relatively enriched in domesticated plants while several bacterial genera were restricted to either wild or cultivated hosts, indicating habitat-associated endophytic specialization. This study provides the first comprehensive assessment of endophytic bacterial diversity in Kenyan Crotalaria species and highlights wild germplasm as an important reservoir of microbial diversity with potential biotechnological value.

title: MLL, TERRA, and telomere chromatin dynamics in replicative senescence and aging.
abstract: Replicative senescence links telomere shortening to irreversible proliferative arrest and is widely recognized as a major tumor-suppressive mechanism. At the organismal level, however, progressive accumulation of senescent cells contributes to tissue dysfunction, chronic inflammation, and aging. Accumulating evidence suggests that telomere shortening influences telomeric and subtelomeric chromatin organization and transcription through mechanisms that remain incompletely understood. Building upon the telomere position effect model of cellular senescence and the subtelomere-telomere theory of aging, this review proposes a chromatin-sensing telomere theory of aging in which telomere shortening contributes to senescence through epigenetic and transcriptional changes at chromosome ends. Central to this model is TERRA, a long non-coding RNA that regulates telomeric chromatin structure, telomere maintenance, and DNA-damage responses. The lysine methyltransferase MLL/KMT2A is a key regulator of TERRA transcription. MLL associates with telomeric chromatin in a telomere length-dependent manner and promotes TERRA transcription through H3K4 methylation. Shelterin components, particularly TRF2, can repress TERRA transcription in certain experimental contexts, and we propose that telomere shortening progressively remodels the shelterin-dependent telomere-subtelomere chromatin environment, potentially reducing access of MLL and RNA polymerase II to subtelomeric promoters. A biphasic model of TERRA regulation is proposed in which early TERRA upregulation in aging tissues promotes telomere protection, while subsequent critical shortening of TERRA-dominant telomeres contributes to reduced TERRA expression, telomere dysfunction, and senescence. This theory proposes a mechanistic link between telomere shortening, chromatin regulation, and quasi-programmed aging.

title: Fusion dsRNA Enhances RNAi Efficiency and Broadens the Insecticidal Spectrum.
abstract: RNA interference (RNAi) technology provides a precise strategy for green control of agricultural pests; however, its low efficiency and high cost still constrain its application. Constructing multitarget fusion dsRNA can significantly improve insecticidal efficiency. Using Tribolium castaneum as a model organism, three highly efficient silencing genes (RpS3, VhaSFD, and EF1) were screened. The results showed that the fusion dsRNA construct dsRVE-3 × 200 bp (200 bp per gene) had the most stable silencing performance, with an LD50 significantly lower than that of the single-gene dsRpS3. Based on the optimized parameters, a fusion dsRNA (named dsNLS) targeting Nilaparvata lugens, Locusta migratoria, and Sogatella furcifera was constructed. dsNLS was significantly superior to naked dsRNA in controlling these three pests, with mortality rates of 69.1%, 71.3%, and 93.4%, respectively, and was safe for nontarget organisms. This study confirms that fusion dsRNA can improve the insecticidal efficiency of RNAi and provides new perspectives for dsRNA design.

title: ROS-dependent phosphorylation of insulin receptor and insulin receptor substrate during pupal diapause development in the cotton bollworm, Helicoverpa armigera.
abstract: Insect diapause is a critical adaptive strategy characterized by developmental arrest and enhanced stress tolerance, orchestrated by intricate molecular networks. The insulin signaling pathway, which governs growth, metabolism, and stress responses, has been implicated in diapause regulation. However, the precise roles of insulin receptor (InR) and insulin receptor substrate (IRS) in modulating pupal diapause remain incompletely understood, particularly in the economically important pest Helicoverpa armigera. Here, we show that InR and IRS are associated with pupal diapause development through redox-sensitive phosphorylation cascades. Temporal profiling revealed a marked upregulation of phosphorylated InR (p-InR) and IRS (p-IRS) in diapause-destined pupal brains, concomitant with elevated phosphorylation of Akt (p-Akt) and ERK (p-ERK). Functional validation in Helicoverpa zea (HzAm1) cells, via overexpression and RNA interference (RNAi), showed that IRS positively regulates Akt and ERK signaling. Further mechanistic studies indicated that reactive oxygen species (ROS) act upstream of the phosphorylation of InR, IRS, Akt, and ERK in vitro and in vivo; these effects were reversible upon ROS scavenging. Further investigations revealed that increased p-ERK was associated with global protein ubiquitination, suggesting this kinase as a key regulator of proteasomal degradation in diapause development. Our findings delineate a ROS-InR-IRS-Akt/ERK signaling framework associated with diapause development and proteostatic regulation in H. armigera, thereby advancing our understanding of insect diapause biology and providing candidate molecular targets for future pest-management interventions.
